frase_gancho.texto: Terraces, walls, and moats to support and defend an entire city.

puente_narrativo.texto: Follow your route: the entry road tells you how passage into this city was controlled.

guion_corto.texto: The city of Xochicalco does not sit on a single hill. Archaeologists speak of three modified hills joined by terraces, and of six lower ones around them where people also lived. To turn those slopes into a city, builders had to cut the rock, fill in gaps, and raise retaining walls. The open spaces were connected by stairways, terraces, and ramps along a north-south axis. UNESCO distinguishes three levels: at the bottom, a residential zone surrounded by walls; in the middle, the market and the largest ball court; at the top, the temples around the Main Plaza. That order is no accident. Whoever climbed was passing from daily life to power and to the sacred.

guion_largo.texto:
Look at the city as a set of steps. Xochicalco rose in a region that was hard to reach, on a series of natural hills, and that was part of its defense.

According to the INAH, the city was founded in the second half of the seventh century on several hills. There was also occupation on six lower hills in the surrounding area. Kenneth Hirth explains that the core was made up of three hills that were modified and connected with terraces.

Achieving this took a great feat of engineering. A conservation study describes how the hill was remodeled by cutting and filling. The terraces and retaining walls created flat spaces for plazas and houses. Stairways, ramps, and terraces link them along a main north-south axis.

UNESCO divides the city into three levels. On the lower level there was a residential zone, surrounded by walls with defended entrances. On the middle level stood a market complex and the largest ball court. On the upper level the temples are grouped around the Main Plaza.

Defense was also written into the landscape. The site director, Medina Romero, mentions a wall four meters high, with bastions and moats, on the south side. Other descriptions speak of ramps, moats, bastions, and forts. A city like this was not conceived for strolling. It was conceived for resisting.

An old detail: Antonio Alzate, who visited the site in seventeen seventy-seven, estimated the main hill at about one hundred seven meters high. It is a measurement from more than two centuries ago, but it shows how much the massive hill impressed him.

Most of the houses on the slopes remain unexcavated. That means what you see is only part of the city. Beneath many terraces there may be more history.

As you walk, notice two things: the walls that hold up the terrain and the way the stairways join one level to another. That is Xochicalco: a city built by hand, stone upon stone, on difficult hills.

texto: Find a retaining wall and notice how it holds up the slope
Count how many levels you can make out from where you are standing
Think about who went up and who stayed below

texto.Location: on a series of natural hills
texto.Levels: lower, middle, and upper, according to UNESCO
texto.South wall: four meters high, with bastions and moats

texto.pregunta: Myth: Xochicalco was built on a single hill.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It rose on several hills that were modified and joined by terraces, and people also lived on lower hills around it.
